Ross Evans: Evans gives Michigan a generational rushing prospect with the vision to see lanes before they open and the elusiveness to make the first defender miss. His acceleration turns those cuts into explosive gains. He has the tools to be the centerpiece of a professional running game.
Raheem Moore: Moore gives Oregon a left-handed quarterback with elite mobility and the instincts to create when the pocket changes shape. His ability to improvise forces defenders to account for both the throw and the run deep into a play. That dual threat gives him franchise-changing upside.
Sam Armstrong: Armstrong pairs a commanding 6-foot-4, 240-pound frame with elite arm talent. The Ohio State quarterback generates velocity effortlessly and can drive the ball into windows downfield. His ability to stretch coverage from the pocket gives him the tools to become the centerpiece of a professional passing game.
Ben Umi: Umi gives UCLA a rare receiving mismatch at 6-foot-8. His athleticism lets him threaten the seam, and his catch radius gives quarterbacks access to throws above a defender’s reach. That combination gives him elite red-zone upside and the tools to command targets near the goal line.
D.J. Quincey: Quincey reads routes early and moves fluidly enough to close on throws before receivers expect him. The LSU corner pairs that anticipation with elite ball-hawking upside, giving the defense a player who can turn tight windows into turnover chances. His instincts stand out among this class’s coverage prospects.
Ha'upu Makaha: Makaha anchors Oregon’s interior front with a 345-pound frame, overwhelming strength and the leverage to control contact. He can hold his ground and shut down running lanes before a back reaches them. That presence gives a defense a nose tackle it can build its run fits around.
Trae Howell: Howell diagnoses runs quickly and arrives with the force to finish tackles for Georgia. His pursuit speed lets him close ground from one sideline to the other, extending his impact beyond the gap in front of him. Those traits give him a strong role in a fast, physical front.
A'Marion Washington: Washington brings rare first-step quickness at 318 pounds and uses powerful hands to clear contact. The Oregon tackle can penetrate from inside and make a quarterback move before the play develops. His burst and strength give a defensive front a disruptive pass-rush option through the middle.
Julian Radford: Radford accelerates quickly into open space and has a feel for improvising when the first option disappears. Kentucky can use his legs on designed runs or let him create after leaving the pocket. That combination gives the offense a dangerous second way to produce explosive plays.
Jalen Wainwright: Wainwright brings length, burst and the bend to turn a tackle’s outside shoulder for Arizona. His pursuit keeps him involved after the play moves away from his initial path. Those traits give him a strong projection as a pass rusher who can pressure quarterbacks from the edge.
